RESOLVED: That the Annual Communication of the Executive Council

The convention was called to order by President Burton at 2 :50 p.m. Recorder

RESOLVED: That it is the wiU of the convention that Article VII of the

On motion duly made and seconded, and following discussion on the wording of

The convention was reconvened by the president at 3 :55 p.m.
Stephen R. Clineburg, Lambda '63, chairman of the Committee on Academic
Standing and Awards, made a temporary report and proposed the following
resolutions :
RESOLVED: That the recorder of this convention be instructed to send
a letter of commendation to the Theta Epsilon Chapter for having attained the

RESOLVED: That the Convention award the permanent plaque and the

RESOLVED: That statements be sent by the Executive Council to both

Rushing Committee B (larger universities), reported that this committee felt

On motion duly adopted, the reading of the minutes of the previous session was

Brother Williams stated that it was the recommendation of his committee that the

Michael A. Laux, Gamma '63, chairman of Rushing Committee A (smaUer
colleges), submitted the committee's report. He stated that the committee does
not find itself concerned with the problem of national fraternity identification, as
reported by Rushing Committee B (larger universities) in the Midwest and Far
West, but that it is concerned with a problem of attitude. He pointed out that it
is the attitude of certain small colleges, certain chapter alumni groups and, most
particularly, the attitude of certain undergraduate members with which the
committee is concerned. He explained that the problem appears to be one of
individual initiative, and the basic failure is a lack of participation inherent both
by alumni and undergraduate brothers in the rushing activities of the chapters.
This, coupled with coUege rushing regulations and restrictions on many small
college campuses, has created an atmosphere somewhat unhealthy for fraternities.
He recommended the endorsement of the recommendations of last year's Rushing
Committee A, which stated: "(1) that the chapter should take a strong stand
against the 100% opportunity system wherever and whenever possible; (2) that,
because of the relatively small active brotherhood (average 37 members), the
entire brotherhood should be required to attend all rushing meetings." He pro
posed the following resolution :
RESOLVED: That the delegates of the 1962 convention relay the feel
ings of this convention to the house presidents and rushing chairmen of the
small college chapters that they investigate the rushing atmosphere on their

campuses and take steps to stimulate the rushing interest of the alumni and
undergraduate brothers.

Appendix B
THE ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
OF THE
EXECUTIVE COUNCIL
TO THE
1962 CONVENTION OF PSI UPSILON
HELD UNDER THE AUSPICES OF THE
DELTA CHAPTER
New York, New York
September 6 and 7, 1962
Your Executive Council takes great pleasure in welcoming the delegates and
visitors to the 120th Convention of Psi Upsilon, held in our 129th year.
Our beloved fraternity was founded at Union College, the mother chapter, in
1833. The Delta founded in 1837 is our second chapter, and it was referred to as
"the first branch of Psi Upsilon" before the chapter designations were estabUshed.
History records that the first convention of the fraternity was held with the Delta
in New York City in 1841. The Delta has also been host to conventions in 1854,
1887 when it celebrated its half-century, and in 1907 and 1932.
This occasion marks the first time that a convention is held in conjunction
with a host chapter's celebration of 125 years in Psi Upsilon. During these 125
years there have been many illustrious alumni of the Delta Chapter. John Taylor
Johnston, 1839, First President of the Metropolitan Museum of Arts, President
of the Council of New York University and generous donor and patron of the
arts; Lawrence H. Mills, 1858, distinguished academic post of Professor of
Philology at Oxford University in England; WiUiam Morgan Kingsley, 1883,
member of the Executive Council 1884-1901, Treasurer of New York University,
President Board of Trustees Union Theological Seminary, President of the United
States Trust Company of New York; The patron saint currently is Dr. Orrin S.
Wightman, '95, a most distinguished medical administrator. The late Judge Edwin
L. Garvin, '97, who was the first President of the Psi Upsilon Alumni Association ;
Frank Jay Gould, '99, recently deceased, who was one of the greatest benefactors
to the university and donor of a large Trust fund to the Delta; Dr. Henry Noble
MacCracken, '00, President Emeritus of Vassar CoUege; Reinald Werrenrath, '05,
famous baritone, now deceased ; Deems Taylor, '06, writer of American opera and
today still in demand by TV and the theater; General William Draper, '16, U. S.
Army, American Ambassador to the Marshall Aid program; General Frank L.
Howley, '25, in charge of the successful Berlin Air Lift and who knew how to talk
to the Russians.
The Delta Corporation, founded November 30, 1896, the alumni sponsoring
body, is one of the strongest alumni bodies of our entire chapter roll, financially
and otherwise.
New York University, host to this convention, has been a pioneering institu
tion for 131 years baring been granted its charter by the State of New York in
1831. It established the first university school of aeronautics, the first university
teacher-training school, and the first laboratory in the nation devoted to bacteriol
ogy and pathology. In the university's old Gothic building at Washington Square,
Page Sixteen

Professor John W. Draper made the first photograph portrait by natural light and
Professor Samuel F. B. Morse perfected the telegraph.
Today New York University includes fifteen coUeges, schools and divisions at
six different centers in Manhattan and the Bronx. It enrolls more than 40,000
students who come from the fifty states and ninety foreign countries. However,
its individual dirisions are smaU enough to assure intimate instruction and ad
visement for every student. A faculty of nearly 4,300 men and women teach
approximately 2,500 courses leading to 30 different degrees.
Many fine buildings comprise the campus of New York University and one
of the most graphically interesting sites is the Hall of Fame for Great Americans,
given by the Psi Upsilon Gould family. New York University's new Research
Center in Westchester wUl be completed shortly. In its Medical School, Jonas
Salk and Albert Sabin developed the two vaccines to prevent the spread of polio.
Ritual and Tradition :
One of the duties of the Executive Council is to furnish the means by which
the traditions and ideals of Psi Upsilon may be carried from one coUege generation
to the next, and so on during the years. In the year just past, your Committee to
Foster, Protect and Preserve Ritual and Tradition has devoted the major part of
its effort to the end that its work along this Une may be more efficient and effective.
The principal means to achieve this end is the visit of a member of Council to a
Chapter. Each year there has been an increasing number of visits made to the
Chapters. However, your Committee has felt that these visits can be made more
productive of good to the Chapters and to the Fraternity as a whole. The
Councillor making such a visit should carry with him a very real and vital message
to the Chapter. The Chapter, in turn, can also bring its problems to the Council
for whatever aid and advice it is possible for it to give.
Currently, much of the material coming out of the Chapter visit is statistical
in nature and can well be obtained through a questionnaire sent prior to the visit.
It is hoped that such visit wiU coincide with a Chapter meeting or made the
occasion for a special meeting at which there will be a full and complete dis
cussion of the affairs of the Fraternity and of the Chapter.
It is our firm belief that visits made in such a basis will be much more
productive of good for aU concerned.
Undergraduate Scholarship:
The foremost objective of the American college and university continues to
be, as it always has been, the inteUectual development of its students. As an
integral part of American higher education, Psi Upsilon stands firmly for the
promotion of intellectual excellence. Every Chapter should keep this objective
as its constant guide, both in the every-day life of its active members and in its

discipline of serious inteUectual effort is short-changing his college, his fraternity,

The Executive Council and the Alumni Association watch the scholastic
attainments of our Chapters with keen and continuing interest. As a means of
emphasizing the vital role of scholarship in undergraduate life and the concern
of the Council and the Alumni Association in fraternity scholarship, the Con
vention of 1949 adopted general resolutions providing for the establishment of
two chapter Scholarship Awards to be presented annually. One award is made
to the Chapter having the highest academic standing for the academic year, the
other to the Chapter evidencing the greatest academic improvement over the
preceding year. The Award for Academic Distinction consists of a cup and a
permanent plaque. The cup is held by the winning Chapter during the ensuing
year and becomes the permanent possession of the Chapter that succeeds in win
ning it for three successive years. The Award for Greatest Improvement consists
of a permanent plaque.

The Executive Council:
The government of this Fraternity is vested in the Convention and in an
Executive Council. The Convention is in session two or three days annually.
For the remainder of the year the Executive Council is the governing body of
the Fratemity, acting under the Constitution.
The Executive Council was instituted in 1869. Past Presidents of the Council
are life members and retired members who have served fifteen years or more MAY
be elected to honorary membership thereon. Living Past Presidents are: Earl
D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93 and Scott Turner, Phi '02. Honorary Members are: Robert
K. Northey, Nu '12 and R. Bourke Corcoran, Omega '15.
AU members serve voluntarily. They pay the expenses of their own meetings,
their traveling expenses in making official chapter visitations and attending con
ventions. Some members regularly travel from Chicago, Montreal, and other
distant points to New York to attend council meetings. Eight well attended
meetings have been held during the past year between October, 1961 and Sep

Special Resolutions
1. RESOLVED: That the 1962 Convention send telegrams of greetings to
Amos Alonzo Stagg, Beta '88, Eari D. Babst, Iota-Phi '93, Scott Turner, Phi '02,
and Edward T. Richards, Sigma '27, and that it express regret to these devoted
brothers that they are unable to attend the convention.
2. RESOLVED: That the recorder of this convention be instructed to send
a letter of commendation to the Theta Epsilon Chapter for having attained the
highest relative scholastic standing in Psi Upsilon for the academic year ended
June, 1961.
3. RESOLVED: That the convention award the permanent plaque and the
rotating cup for the academic year ended June, 1961, to the Rho Chapter for its
outstanding academic achievement.
4. RESOLVED: That the award for academic improvement be awarded the
Omicron Chapter for its significant improvement during the academic year ended
June, 1961.
5. RESOLVED: That each chapter establish and implement a schedule of
regular meetings with its faculty adviser.
6. RESOLVED: That, insofar as critics of the fraternity system are en
couraged in their attacks by low academic standing of individual fraternities, the
convention of 1962 go on record that a primary responsibility of each chapter of
Psi Upsilon be to maintain as high an academic standing as possible.
7. RESOLVED : That the recorder be instructed to send the presidents of
the alumni body and undergraduate chapter of the Kappa, Xi, Omega and Theta
Epsilon Chapters letters expressing the convention's regret and appallment at the
absence of delegates and at the lack of reasons presented for such absences.
8. RESOLVED: That each new member, immediately following his initia
tion, be required to familiarize himself with the spirit of the Psi Upsilon Fra
ternity, as expressed in Article VII of the Constitution of Psi Upsilon.
9. RESOLVED: That the delegates of the 1962 convention relay the feel
ings of this convention to the house presidents and rushing chairmen of the smaU
college chapters that they investigate the rushing atmosphere on their campuses
and take steps to stimulate the rushing interest of the alumni and undergraduate
brothers.
10. RESOLVED: That a letter be sent to the Delta Delta Chapter of Psi
Upsilon, in which it is suggested that it contact aU other fraternities on this
campus urging them to communicate with their alumni to exert severe pressure
on the Williams administration to abandon any intentions it may have towards
eliminating fraternities as they presently exist on said campus.
